clue.text: Safe Lincoln with fat French philosopher

parts.note: peter is old criminal slang for a safe, as cracked by a peterman
Abe is the familiar name of Abraham Lincoln, the US president
lard is pig fat used in cooking

explanation.surface: A dependable Lincoln, plus a plump Frenchman with a taste for ideas.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Safe' looks like an adjective meaning secure, but it is the noun: PETER is underworld slang for a strongbox.
explanation.definitionFit: The twelfth-century scholastic thinker, famous for his love affair with Héloïse, taught logic and theology in Paris.

clue.text: Versatile prophet overturned in some suet or pudding mix

indicators.note: turned upside down, which in a down entry means the letters are read from bottom to top
the letters sought are found inside some of the words that follow, spanning the gaps

explanation.surface: A recipe instruction for a steamed pudding with suet, oddly featuring a seer.
explanation.walkthrough: Inside 'suet or p(udding)' run SUETORP; 'overturned' reads it backwards.
explanation.definitionFit: In Greek myth the old sea-god could foretell the future and changed shape at will, hence the adjective for adaptability.

clue.text: Betjeman's was blackish-brown

parts.note: recalls a row of houses in John Betjeman's 'Parliament Hill Fields', where the tram rocks past Zwanziger the baker's and a sooty Kentish Town row

explanation.walkthrough: The line is 'Rocked past Zwanziger the baker's, and the terrace blackish brown' from Betjeman's 1945 poem about a tram ride through Kentish Town, north London.
explanation.definitionFit: In the poem the sooty row of joined houses is described with exactly that colour.

clue.text: Do this, and be damned again, Wellington may have thought

definitions.text: Do this, and be damned again, Wellington may have thought

parts.words: Do this, and be damned again, Wellington may have thought
parts.note: plays on the Duke of Wellington's reply to a blackmailer threatening to print his mistress's memoirs: 'Publish and be damned'

explanation.walkthrough: Wellington's famous retort was 'Publish and be damned'; doing it a second time would mean bringing the book out once more.
explanation.definitionFit: To issue a printed work again is the action, with the prefix for 'again' added to Wellington's verb.

clue.text: County for Georgette Heyer's Regency one?

definitions.meaning: The usual short form of Buckinghamshire, an English county west of London
Heyer's novel 'Regency Buck' has a dandy of the period as its hero; the plural answer is a set of such fops

explanation.walkthrough: BUCKS is short for Buckinghamshire, an English county; a buck was a Regency dandy, as in Heyer's novel 'Regency Buck'. The question mark marks the second definition as an example.
explanation.definitionFit: Both senses fit: the abbreviated name of a home county, and dashing young men of fashion in Regency England.

clue.text: Ludwig repeatedly made overtures to her (him?)

definitions.text: Ludwig repeatedly made overtures to her (him?)

parts.words: Ludwig repeatedly made overtures to her (him?)
parts.note: Beethoven wrote three overtures named after the heroine of his only opera, who spends it disguised as the young man Fidelio

explanation.walkthrough: 'Made overtures' suggests courting, but Ludwig van Beethoven literally composed several overtures (Nos 1-3) named for this heroine; '(him?)' points to her disguise as a man.
explanation.definitionFit: She is the wife in 'Fidelio' who disguises herself as a male jailer's assistant to rescue her husband.

clue.text: Middle-period Lawrence in Italy finds composer

parts.note: T. E. Lawrence enlisted in the RAF under the name John Hume Ross in the middle of his life
taken as written
I is the international vehicle code for Italy

explanation.surface: A biographer notes that D. H. Lawrence's middle years, spent in Italy, reveal a composer.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests D. H. Lawrence, who lived in Italy; the wordplay wants T. E. Lawrence (of Arabia), who called himself Ross in the 1920s.
explanation.definitionFit: Gioachino Rossini wrote 'The Barber of Seville' and 'William Tell', so he is an Italian opera composer.

clue.text: Paris girl with roll of notes joining fellow novelist, produced 1 Across

parts.note: Helen of Troy was the woman Paris carried off, starting the Trojan War
a wad is a thick roll of banknotes
Ethel M. Dell was a popular English writer of romantic novels

explanation.surface: A Parisian girl with a bankroll teams up with another writer of fiction.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Paris girl' suggests a Frenchwoman, but this Paris is the Trojan prince. 'Fellow' marks Dell as a fellow novelist; 'joining' links the pieces. The definition stands for 'one who produced' the novel 'Peter Abelard' (1933).
explanation.definitionFit: The Irish scholar wrote the 1933 historical novel about the medieval logician and Héloïse.

clue.text: "Staying in swanky hotels,— -ping, partying, generally overindulging" (Small World, David Lodge)

definitions.text: "Staying in swanky hotels,— -ping, partying, generally overindulging" (Small World, David Lodge)

parts.words: "Staying in swanky hotels,— -ping, partying, generally overindulging" (Small World, David Lodge)
parts.note: a fill-in-the-blank quotation from Lodge's campus novel about globetrotting academics; the gap takes a phrase for self-indulgent behaviour

explanation.walkthrough: The gap plus '-ping' makes a word for indulging in self-glorifying travel, which suits Lodge's conference-hopping professors.
explanation.definitionFit: A self-indulgent jaunt that inflates one's own importance is what the dons in the novel enjoy.

clue.text: Credit to old English South American makes a wealthy man

parts.note: CR is the standard abbreviation for credit in accounts
US stands for American, as in US troops

explanation.surface: Lending money to an elderly Englishman and a South American produces a rich man.
explanation.walkthrough: 'South American' looks like one thing, a person from South America, but splits into S and US.
explanation.definitionFit: The king of Lydia was proverbially rich, so his name stands for any very rich person.

clue.text: Starting with marriage, she finally reached her destiny

definitions.text: Starting with marriage, she finally reached her destiny

parts.words: Starting with marriage, she finally reached her destiny
parts.note: a Scottish novelist whose first book was 'Marriage' (1818) and whose last was 'Destiny' (1831)

explanation.walkthrough: It reads like a woman's life story, but 'marriage' and 'destiny' are the titles of the first and last of her three novels.
explanation.definitionFit: The Edinburgh writer published 'Marriage', 'The Inheritance' and 'Destiny', the first and last named in the clue.

clue.text: Nathan's metaphor for Bath-sheba

parts.note: in 2 Samuel 12 the prophet Nathan rebukes King David with a parable of a rich man who takes a poor man's only young female sheep

explanation.walkthrough: Nathan's parable has a rich man seize a poor man's one pet animal, standing for David taking Uriah's wife Bath-sheba.
explanation.definitionFit: The poor man's single cherished young female sheep in the parable represents Uriah's wife.

clue.text: Some of Pain's were in the dark

definitions.text: Some of Pain's were in the dark

parts.words: Some of Pain's were in the dark
parts.note: refers to Barry Pain, English humorist, whose 1901 collection of tales was titled '... in the Dark'

explanation.walkthrough: 'Pain' looks like suffering, but it is the writer Barry Pain, whose book 'Stories in the Dark' gives the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Barry Pain's volume of short tales has the plural noun followed by 'in the Dark' as its title.

clue.text: Some trash from Robert Herrick?

definitions.meaning: rubbish or refuse, material thrown away
the American novelist Robert Herrick published a novel with this title in 1924

explanation.walkthrough: The surface points to the Cavalier poet Robert Herrick, but the second definition is the American novelist of that name, whose 1924 novel bears this title.
explanation.definitionFit: Refuse is discarded rubbish, and the same single word names the novel by the American Robert Herrick.

clue.text: An impression of Robert Lowell

definitions.meaning: an impression is an impersonation or copy of someone
Lowell's 1961 book '...' gathered his free versions of European poems, so each one is a single example

explanation.walkthrough: Lowell's collection 'Imitations' (1961) gives the second sense; each poem in it is one.
explanation.definitionFit: A mimic's impression is a copy of someone, and Lowell's loose translations were published as such copies.

clue.text: "Spontaneous" musical work probably well rehearsed

definitions.meaning: done without preparation, off the cuff
a short piano piece with an improvised character, as by Schubert or Chopin, which a performer will in fact have practised

explanation.walkthrough: The quotation marks around 'Spontaneous' hint at the irony: a concert piece of this kind sounds improvised but has been practised carefully.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means unrehearsed, and it also names a piano piece in a free, improvisatory style.

clue.text: Phased hit reworked by B. Traven

indicators.note: reworked means the letters of the preceding words are shaped into a new order

explanation.surface: A phased hit single gets remixed by a mysterious novelist.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Reworked' rearranges PHASED HIT. The definition stands for 'a work by' B. Traven, the elusive author of 'The Treasure of the Sierra Madre'.
explanation.definitionFit: Traven's 1926 novel follows a stateless sailor on a doomed tramp steamer.

clue.text: Aria and medley for Mrs Antipholus

indicators.note: a medley is a mixture, so the letters of the two words are mixed together

explanation.surface: An aria and a medley are performed for an operatic wife.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Medley' looks like a musical term beside 'Aria', but it signals that ARIA and AND are mixed. 'For' links to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: In 'The Comedy of Errors' she is married to Antipholus of Ephesus.

clue.text: His castle may be seen at Alnwick

definitions.text: His castle may be seen at Alnwick

parts.words: His castle may be seen at Alnwick
parts.note: Alnwick Castle in Northumberland stood in for the wizarding school in the Harry Potter films, so the castle belongs to one of the school's founders

explanation.walkthrough: Alnwick Castle, in Northumberland in north-east England, was the film location for the wizarding school, read here as the castle of a man.
explanation.definitionFit: The school's name read as a possessive makes it a person, whose castle was filmed in Northumberland.

clue.text: Writer of poems (he includes German one)

indicators.note: includes means the first piece holds the second inside it

parts.note: taken as written
ein is German for one

explanation.surface: A bracketed aside notes a poet who slips in a German word.
explanation.walkthrough: The bracket reads as an aside about the poet, but its words are the wordplay; 'includes' signals a container, with the German numeral inside.
explanation.definitionFit: Heinrich Heine wrote the lyric poems set by Schubert and Schumann.

clue.text: Goddess conceals approximate arrival time for courtesan

indicators.note: conceals means the goddess's name hides the other piece within it

parts.note: Hera is the Greek queen of the gods
ETA stands for estimated time of arrival

explanation.surface: A goddess keeps quiet about when she'll roughly turn up for a lady of pleasure.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Approximate arrival time' is the airline abbreviation for an estimate; 'conceals' signals that the goddess's name goes round it.
explanation.definitionFit: In ancient Greece the word named an educated, high-class mistress or kept woman.

clue.text: "… utterly indifferent to her having any cultivation: having no modern idea respecting feminine capacities" (Doctor Grimshaw's Secret, Hawthorne)

definitions.text: "… utterly indifferent to her having any cultivation: having no modern idea respecting feminine capacities" (Doctor Grimshaw's Secret, Hawthorne)

parts.words: "… utterly indifferent to her having any cultivation: having no modern idea respecting feminine capacities" (Doctor Grimshaw's Secret, Hawthorne)
parts.note: a fill-in quotation from Hawthorne's unfinished romance; the missing verb says the doctor had absorbed no modern idea

explanation.walkthrough: The gap sits in 'having (imbibed) no modern idea', where the verb means taken in or absorbed.
explanation.definitionFit: The verb of drinking in, used figuratively for taking ideas into the mind, fills the blank.

clue.text: Poet gets measure correct

parts.note: an en is a printer's unit of measure
right means correct

explanation.surface: A poet takes the right measurements.
explanation.walkthrough: An en is a printing measure, half an em. D. J. Enright was a twentieth-century English poet.
explanation.definitionFit: D. J. Enright was an English poet, editor and critic of the Movement generation.

clue.text: Youngster has right to wooden artefacts

indicators.note: has means the first piece holds the second within it

parts.note: a teen is a teenager, a youngster

explanation.surface: A youngster has the right to some carved woodwork.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Has' puts R inside TEEN; 'to' links to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Small domestic objects turned or carved from timber, such as bowls and platters, are collected under this name.

clue.text: Bridges constructed last month

parts.note: the poet laureate Robert Bridges published '... and Other Poems' in 1920, so 'Bridges' is the man, not spans

explanation.walkthrough: 'Bridges constructed' sounds like engineering, but Robert Bridges, poet laureate, composed a poem with this month for its title. The month is late in the year rather than the last one.
explanation.definitionFit: Robert Bridges' 1920 collection was named after the tenth month of the year.

clue.text: "If find… camp followers waiting for us at the other end, I'll know there's been a—" (Brideshead Revisited)

definitions.text: "If find… camp followers waiting for us at the other end, I'll know there's been a—" (Brideshead Revisited)

parts.words: "If find… camp followers waiting for us at the other end, I'll know there's been a—" (Brideshead Revisited)
parts.note: a fill-in quotation from Waugh's novel: an officer suspects secret troop movements have been given away

explanation.walkthrough: In the wartime frame of 'Brideshead Revisited', an officer says that finding camp followers waiting would mean information had escaped.
explanation.definitionFit: An unauthorised disclosure of secret information is a seeping out, like liquid through a crack.

clue.text: Historian finds smooth stone in river? Quite the reverse

indicators.note: in would put the stone inside the river, but the next words reverse the containment
quite the reverse swaps the roles just described, so the river goes inside the stone

parts.note: a pebble is a small stone smoothed by water

explanation.surface: A historian discovers a smooth stone in a river, or is it the other way round?
explanation.walkthrough: 'Quite the reverse' turns 'stone in river' into 'river in stone': R inside PEBBLE. John Prebble wrote popular histories of the Scottish Highlands.
explanation.definitionFit: John Prebble wrote 'Culloden' and 'The Highland Clearances', so he is a popular historian.

clue.text: His work was becoming French

parts.note: the French novelist's first book was titled 'Devenir!', French for 'becoming', and he wrote in French

explanation.walkthrough: 'Becoming' seems to mean 'turning into', but it translates 'Devenir!', the 1909 debut novel of Roger Martin du Gard, Nobel laureate of 1937.
explanation.definitionFit: Roger Martin du Gard, author of 'Les Thibault', published 'Devenir!' as his first novel.
